title: Seven conditions of welfare
hook: the last journey begins: a people thrives while it meets often and in harmony

segments.voice: Yesterday: a teaching that looked clear and wasn't, and your line, don't say that, Ananda. What did you look at twice? Today we begin the longest discourse of all, and we'll walk it for a week. Day five hundred forty-five.

A king wants a war. Ajatasattu of Magadha, the same king who rode out on a moonlit night a few weeks back on this path, has decided to crush the Vajjians, a confederation of clans to the north. Before he marches, he sends his chief minister, Vassakara, to the Buddha on Vulture's Peak, with orders: tell him my plan, and bring back exactly what he says. A Buddha does not speak falsely. So the minister arrives, bows, and lays out the plan. And the Buddha doesn't answer him. He turns to Ananda, who is standing behind him, fanning him. Today: Mahaparinibbana.
screen: `A KING WANTS A WAR.` → `THE MINISTER ON VULTURE'S PEAK.` → `THE BUDDHA TURNS TO ANANDA.`

segments.voice: The discourse is the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the great discourse on the final passing, the account of the Buddha's last months. Maha means great. Parinibbana is the complete going out, the death of one already awakened. It begins, of all places, with politics. Ananda, the Buddha asks, have you heard that the Vajjians meet often, and in large numbers? I have, sir. Then, as long as they do, they can be expected to grow, not decline. And he goes through seven questions. Do they meet in harmony, rise in harmony, and do their business in harmony? Do they keep to the rules they've agreed and not invent new ones out of nowhere? Do they honor and listen to their elders? Do they refrain from carrying off women and girls by force? Do they honor their shrines? Do they protect those who live the holy life among them? Seven yeses, seven reasons to thrive. The minister gets the message. The Vajjians, he says, can't be beaten in war, only by diplomacy or by splitting them apart. And he goes. Then the Buddha calls the monks together and gives them seven conditions of their own, starting the same way: as long as you meet often, and in harmony, you can be expected to grow, not decline. Notice what comes first. Not doctrine. Not meditation. Meeting. People who keep showing up, and who leave on good terms. The great final journey of the Buddha opens with a lesson about how communities stay alive.
screen: `MAHAPARINIBBANA: THE GREAT FINAL PASSING.` · `SEVEN QUESTIONS ABOUT THE VAJJIANS.` · `ONLY BEATEN BY SPLITTING THEM.` · `THE SAME SEVEN FOR THE MONKS.` · then, large: `MEET OFTEN, IN HARMONY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and call to mind the people you belong with: a family, a team, a group of friends, a congregation, a neighborhood. Picture the last time you were all together. Was it often enough? Did you leave in harmony? Let one face come up whom you haven't seen in a while. Breathe with that face for a moment, and hold one wish for that group: may we keep meeting. After the bell, if you like, set one gathering on the calendar. The bell holds the time.
Mahaparinibbana. The great final passing, the name of the longest Long Discourse, the story of the Buddha's last journey. Today's word.
Your line: meet often, in harmony. Today, reach out to one group you belong to and suggest getting together, and when you do meet, try to leave on good terms. Day five hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Buddhist monastic communities meet regularly, most visibly at the fortnightly uposatha gathering where the monastic rules are recited, and many lay groups keep weekly sittings and study meetings.

fork.setup: you're the king's minister. you've heard seven reasons the Vajjians will thrive. what do you report?
options: that they can be beaten easily.
that they can't be beaten in war, only by diplomacy or by splitting them.
that the Buddha refused to answer.
fork.reveal: Vassakara concludes the Vajjians can't be conquered by war while they keep the seven, only by diplomacy or dividing them.

original.note: Pali mahaparinibbana: maha, great; parinibbana, the complete passing of an awakened one.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha's last discourse is all about death.
what it means: it opens with seven conditions that keep a people, and then the monks, from decline.
what a scholar hears: DN 16, the longest sutta in the Pali canon, sets the satta aparihaniya dhamma (seven conditions of non-decline) at its start, first for the Vajjians and then for the Sangha.
